1.pericope_label: Why boastest thou thyself in mischief, O mighty man? thy tongue deviseth mischiefs

schools.summary: Augustine notes that the title names the priest by one form and the history by another, reports that his manuscripts kept the title form, and turns the discrepancy into a rule, that a change of name should make the reader more intent on a mystery rather than pursuing the apparent facts of history and despising the sacred veilings.

Calvin refers the psalm to the terror that followed the killing of the priests and to the informer triumphing in his success, and explains the term in the heading as marking psalms in which David records a chastisement sent like a schoolmaster’s rod; Gill reads the boasting forward as the character of antichrist, who boasts of merit and of works of supererogation and of blood shed in supposed service to God.

Spurgeon raises the possibility that the address is aimed past the informer at the king, in which case it is spoken pityingly, holds that honourable titles are irony where the wearer is cruel, and gives the razor two senses, the barber who makes a man bald unawares and the throat cut under pretence of shaving; Henry makes the informer mighty by office rather than by strength and says it is no honour for those that wear a sword to hector those that wear an ephod.

Clarke rehearses the history at length, reports that all the versions but one agree with the title, objects that the psalm is too mild in composition for the most barbarous transaction on record, itemises the offender’s character in seven counts, and reads the razor as the instrument that wounds instead of shaving; Wesley supplies the sarcasm outright, O valiant captain, to kill a few weak and unarmed persons.

Ellicott renders the title of address as hero used sarcastically but rejects on grammatical grounds the older versions making him a hero at mischief, and glosses the devouring words as words that swallow down a neighbour’s life, honour and goods; Keil and Delitzsch defend the inscription as one of eight assigning psalms to the persecution by Saul, some verifiable and none replaceable by anything more credible.

debates: Is the title trustworthy, and whom does the psalm address? Keil and Delitzsch defend the inscriptions of this group as verifiable in part and irreplaceable in the rest; Clarke notes that all the versions but one agree with the title, yet objects that the psalm is too mild for the atrocity it is said to answer; Augustine finds the priest named differently in title and history and makes the discrepancy a reason to look for a mystery rather than a correction; Spurgeon suggests the address may reach past the informer to the king himself, and be spoken in pity.
outliers: Augustine holds that a changed name in a psalm title should make the reader the more intent upon a mystery, lest he pursue the apparent facts of history and despise the sacred veilings.
Henry answers the title of mighty man with the observation that it is no honour for those that wear a sword to hector those that wear an ephod.

Clarke breaks the offender’s character into seven numbered counts, from boasting in the power to do evil to a tongue that professed friendship while the heart was full of enmity, and then turns to the punishment.
Spurgeon sets the tyrant’s fury against the perennial stream of divine mercy, observing that if priests be slain their Master lives.
themes: boasting treated as worse than the deed boasted of
a title of honour turned into sarcasm
a discrepancy of names read as an invitation to allegory
the tongue figured as a razor in a barber’s hand
words that swallow a neighbour whole

5.pericope_label: God shall likewise destroy thee for ever: lo, this is the man that made not God his strength

schools.summary: Spurgeon keeps both awe and laughter, the latter being contempt at deep schemes all baffled rather than merriment, and warns that wealth and wickedness combined make a monster; Henry insists the laughter is rational and serious rather than ludicrous, and notes that the psalmist puts the triumph in the mouth of other righteous persons lest it look like personal revenge.

Gill notes that the word for destroy is used of breaking down a house infected with leprosy and takes it of the extinction of the informer’s family, gives the Aramaic paraphrase that makes the strength refused the Word of the Lord, and sets those who run to God as a strong hold against the rich man whose wealth is his strong city.

Clarke distributes the sentence into three acts of demolition, prefers a variant reading found in three manuscripts and one version that has the righteous rejoice rather than fear, and turns the epitaph into a general warning about money, asking where the religious man is whose piety has not declined as his wealth multiplied, and prescribing open hands to the poor; Wesley presses the suddenness of the uprooting and glosses the fear as reverence for a just judgment.

Ellicott renders the second verb as laying hold of a live coal from the hearth and observes that the sense is the exact opposite of plucking a brand from the burning, being rather the pulling apart of the house-fire and the extinguishing of domestic life, and finds the mingled awe and exultation of the righteous finely described; Keil and Delitzsch set the uprooted betrayer against the betrayed as a green olive planted in inaccessible ground.

debates: Do the righteous fear or rejoice at the fall? Clarke reports three manuscripts and one ancient version reading they shall rejoice, holds this the true text since laughter follows immediately and belongs with rejoicing rather than dread, and would emend accordingly; Ellicott keeps the received reading and holds that the mingled awe at the fall and exultation at the overthrow are finely caught; Wesley and Henry gloss the fear as reverence for a just judgment, and Spurgeon keeps both feelings in order, awe first and then contemptuous laughter.
outliers: Ellicott points out that the verb here is the exact reverse of the familiar phrase about plucking a brand from the burning, the picture being of a house-fire pulled apart and domestic life extinguished.

Clarke quotes a Latin line that the love of money grows precisely as the money grows, asks where the religious man is in whose hands wealth has multiplied without piety declining in the same proportion, and prescribes opening both hands to the poor as the only remedy.
Henry guards the passage against vindictiveness by noting that the psalmist does not claim the triumph as his own act but assigns it to other righteous persons.
themes: a sentence unpacked verb by verb
a coal raked from the hearth rather than rescued from it
a textual variant that changes the moral of the verse
wealth named as the thing trusted instead of God

8.pericope_label: But I am like a green olive tree in the house of God: I will praise thee for ever

schools.summary: Gill supplies the future tense, since the speaker was then an exile from the house of God, making the verse a confidence rather than a description, and lists the properties of the olive as a choice and fruitful tree, evergreen and durable, its branches symbols of peace.

Clarke also reads the verse as future, denies outright that olive trees were planted in the house of God and takes the comparison as one of proper soil and situation, sets the poisonous tree pulled up by the roots against the healthy olive bearing fruit, refers the last clause to all his good coming from God, and turns the waiting into a practice of using the ordinances with the saints; Wesley refers the same clause concretely to the destruction of the enemies and the establishing of the throne, of which he is as assured as if it were done.

Ellicott corrects the epithet green to vigour rather than colour, since olive foliage cannot be called verdant, quotes a naturalist on how the same tree looks to an eastern eye, notes that the olive alternates with the vine as an emblem of a prosperous nation, and holds it quite possible that trees really stood in the temple precincts as they do there now; Keil and Delitzsch make the sacred and inaccessible ground the point of the figure and refer the last clause to the purpose of David’s election.

debates: Were there trees in the house of God? Clarke states flatly that the verse does not mean olive trees were planted there, only that the man stood in God’s house as the olive stands in its proper soil; Ellicott holds it quite possible that trees actually grew in the temple precincts, as they do in the same enclosure now, so that a rendering near the house of God would state a literal fact, while allowing the figure may be wholly figurative.

What has God done, in the last verse? Keil and Delitzsch refer it to the carrying out of what was aimed at in the election of David; Wesley makes it the destruction of the enemies and the establishing of the throne, spoken of as assured though still future; Clarke keeps it general, that all his good comes from God.
outliers: Ellicott concedes that the olive is scarcely a beautiful tree to Western eyes and quotes a naturalist for whom its pale foliage, spread like a silver sea along the slopes of the hills, speaks of peace and plenty and gladness.
Clarke makes waiting on the name a practice rather than a posture, expecting the continuation of blessing through uniting with the saints in the ordinances.
themes: a present tense read as a future confidence
a tree praised for vigour rather than colour
a figure suspected of being literal
two trees set against each other, uprooted and planted
a deliverance given thanks for before it arrives
